:::{#exm-exponential-decay}
#### The same factor over two run lengths

Take $s^{(0)} = 0.1$ and $\decay = 0.99$.
The [step length](#def-exponential-decay) after $1000$ updates and after $100000$ updates is:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### R

```{r}
#| label: exponential-decay-r
#| code-fold: false
s0_ed <- 0.1
decay_ed <- 0.99
t_ed <- c(1000, 100000)
data.frame(t = t_ed, step_length = s0_ed * decay_ed^t_ed)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: exponential-decay-python
#| code-fold: false
s0_ed, decay_ed = 0.1, 0.99
for t_ed in [1000, 100000]:
    print(t_ed, s0_ed * decay_ed ** t_ed);
```

:::

After $1000$ updates the step length is about $4.3 \times 10^{-6}$, <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
and after $100000$ updates it is $0$ in floating-point arithmetic.
One factor gives two very different schedules.

<!-- no-figure: the example tabulates two step lengths -->

:::
